'''Hans-Dieter Beckey''' (8 June 1921 – 18 June 1992<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.uni-bonn.de/die-universitaet/historischer-kalender/2017/historischer-kalender-2017|title = Universität}}</ref>) was a German physicist and mass spectrometry researcher known for his work on [[field desorption]].<ref name="encyclopedia">{{cite book |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/book/9780081003794/the-encyclopedia-of-mass-spectrometry |title=The Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry |isbn=9780081003794 |format= |accessdate= |last1=Nier |first1=Keith A. |last2=Yergey |first2=Alfred L. |last3=Jane Gale |first3=P. |date=6 May 2015 |publisher=Elsevier Science }}</ref>

==Career and Research==
Beckey graduated from the [[University of Hamburg]] in 1950 and then received his PhD in the group of [[Wilhelm Groth]] at the [[University of Bonn]] in 1952.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He wrote his [[habilitation]] in 1959 and became full professor of physical chemistry at the University of Bonn in 1966.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> In 1958, he used [[field ionization]] (FI) together with [[mass spectrometry]] to transfer ions into the gas phase. Using high field strengths, he was able to show that FI could ionize labile molecules that were not amenable to [[electron ionization]] (EI) due to the latter's propensity to fragment ions.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He thus established FI as a complementary technique to EI.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He also showed that FI is suited to study the decomposition kinetics of organic molecules in the gas phase.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> However, his most important contribution to mass spectrometry was the invention of [[field desorption]], a [[soft ionization]] technique suitable for large molecules including [[biopolymer]]s. After his illness forced him to cease working, his co-worker [[Hans-Rolf Schulten]] continued this work.

Beckey received the [[Nernst Prize]] (now the Nernst–Haber–Bodenstein Prize) from the German Bunsen Society for Physical
Chemistry in 1964.<ref name="encyclopedia"/>

Beckey was married to Gudrun Kischke (in 1951) and they had three children.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He was forced to resign in 1979 due to an illness that had acquired in 1969.<ref name="encyclopedia"/> He died in 1992.
